title: Regenerative Braking Shunt Choppers, CAN-FD CRC-16 + Rolling-Counter Watchdogs & SIL/HIL Fault Injection

blocks.x: This is the dedicated Track 07 Tier 2 bridge module before Step 2.8 (`07-systems.T2.08`, the Tier 2 Boss Capstone). When your custom 4-layer $24\text{ V}/15\text{ A}$ CAN-FD servo (`01-electronics.T2.02` + `04-embedded.T2.05`) decelerates a heavy link or Furuta pendulum arm rapidly (`06-robotics.T2.07`), the motor acts as a generator and pumps kinetic energy back into the DC bus. Because bench power supplies have series output protection diodes and cannot sink reverse current, an unclamped stop from $30\text{ rad/s}$ spikes a $24\text{ V}$ bus above $160\text{ V}$ in milliseconds! Before running the Tier 2 Boss Capstone, you must size an **active hysteretic shunt brake chopper** (`MOSFET + power resistor`), protect every CAN-FD command frame with a **CRC-16 checksum, 4-bit rolling counter, and hardware Window Watchdog (`WWDG`) timeout**, and verify fault recovery via **Software/Hardware-in-the-Loop (SIL/HIL) fault injection**. Already know this? Take the Skip test or the Ladder Gate test in section 7 first.
Three systems-engineering barriers separate a benchtop demo from an industrial-grade custom servo drive:

items.x: **Regenerative Braking & Active Shunt Brake Chopper:** When torque $\tau$ and velocity $\omega$ have opposite signs ($P_{\text{mech}} = \tau\omega < 0$), the motor converts mechanical kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2}J\omega_0^2$ into electrical charge on the DC bus capacitor $C_{\text{bus}}$. Without a return path, capacitor energy $\frac{1}{2}C_{\text{bus}}(V_{\text{peak}}^2 - V_{\text{nom}}^2) = \eta E_k$ forces $V_{\text{peak}}$ to skyrocket. An **active shunt brake chopper** places a low-side MOSFET + power resistor $R_{\text{brake}}$ across the DC bus: a hardware comparator or ADC watchdog turns the MOSFET ON whenever $V_{\text{bus}} \ge V_{\text{on}}$ (e.g. $27.5\text{ V}$) and OFF when $V_{\text{bus}} \le V_{\text{off}}$ ($25.5\text{ V}$), burning the regenerated kinetic energy safely as heat in $R_{\text{brake}}$!

**CAN-FD End-to-End Integrity (`CRC-16` + `4-Bit Rolling Counter` + `Window Watchdog`):** What if a loose connector freezes the last `MIT Mode` torque packet in a buffer (`stale data`), or EMI flips bits on the bus? Every command frame adds an application-layer **4-bit rolling counter** (`0..15` incrementing by $+1 \pmod{16}$ each tick) plus a **16-bit CRC**, monitored by a hardware **Window Watchdog (`WWDG`)** that trips to zero-torque damping if $> N_{\text{miss}}$ consecutive frames arrive late or corrupted.

**SIL/HIL Fault Injection Matrix:** Never wait for an accidental crash to discover whether your over-voltage, encoder-open, or CAN-timeout handlers work! A **SIL/HIL Fault Injection Matrix** systematically injects each fault (open encoder SPI `MISO`, drop 5 consecutive CAN frames, inject a $+5\text{ V}$ bus surge) and verifies that the drive transitions to a safe state within its deterministic fault reaction time budget $t_{\text{react}} \le t_{\text{max}}$.
**Unclamped Regenerative Voltage Surge & Shunt Brake Resistor Sizing:**

**Unclamped Peak Voltage:** When rotor inertia $J$ decelerates from $\omega_0$ to $0\text{ rad/s}$ with net regeneration efficiency $\eta \in (0, 1]$ into bus capacitance $C_{\text{bus}}$ starting at $V_{\text{nom}}$:

**Maximum Brake Resistor Bound:** To absorb peak regenerative power $P_{\text{regen,peak}} = \eta |\tau_{\max} \omega_0|$ while keeping the bus clamped at or below $V_{\text{clamp}}$, the shunt brake resistor $R_{\text{brake}}$ must dissipate at least $P_{\text{regen,peak}}$ at voltage $V_{\text{clamp}}$:
**CAN-FD Rolling-Counter Continuity & Watchdog Timeout Budget:**

Given 4-bit counter $c_k \in \{0, \dots, 15\}$, the modular step difference between consecutive received frames is $\Delta c_k = (c_k - c_{k-1}) \bmod 16$. A valid sequential stream has $\Delta c_k = 1$; $\Delta c_k = 0$ indicates a **frozen/duplicate frame**, while $1 < \Delta c_k \le N_{\text{max-drop}}$ indicates $\Delta c_k - 1$ dropped frames.
For nominal frame period $T_{\text{cmd}}$ (e.g., $1.0\text{ ms}$) and maximum tolerated consecutive missed frames $N_{\text{miss}}$ (e.g., $3$), the watchdog timeout window is:
**SIL/HIL Fault-Injection Coverage & Safe Reaction Margin:**

Across a catalog of $F_{\text{total}}$ required fault modes (Over-Voltage, Over-Current, Encoder SPI CRC Loss, CAN Watchdog Timeout, Thermal $I^2t$ Derating), fault-injection coverage is $C_{\text{hil}} = F_{\text{passed}} / F_{\text{total}}$, and every fault $i$ must satisfy measured reaction latency $t_{\text{react},i} \le t_{\text{budget},i}$.

blocks.x: **Predict first (before you run it):** Commit to four numbers and one ordering. (1) With $J = 0.04\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$, $\omega_0 = 30.0\text{ rad/s}$ and $\eta = 0.75$, how much energy reaches the bus - near $13.5\text{ J}$ or near $18.0\text{ J}$? (2) Dumped into $C_{\text{bus}} = 1000\ \mu\text{F}$ from $24.0\text{ V}$, does that push the bus to roughly $166\text{ V}$ or to roughly $40\text{ V}$? (3) Is $R_{\text{brake,max}}$ an upper bound or a target, and does a $4.0\ \Omega$ part sit inside it? (4) Which is the more serious protocol fault, a duplicate frame ($4 \to 4$) or a five-count jump ($4 \to 10$)? Two tells that a wrong answer is a mistake rather than a different convention: an unclamped voltage below $48\text{ V}$ means the $\frac{1}{2}J\omega^2$ term was divided instead of added under the square root (the surge can only *raise* the bus); and a resistor bound below $4.0\ \Omega$ means $\eta$ was applied twice, since $P_{\text{regen,peak}} = \eta|\tau_{\max}\omega_0| = 180.0\text{ W}$ already contains it.

Size a regenerative shunt brake chopper for a $24\text{ V}$ custom servo decelerating $J = 0.04\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ from $\omega_0 = 30.0\text{ rad/s}$ ($\tau_{\max} = 8.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}, \eta = 0.75, C_{\text{bus}} = 1000\ \mu\text{F}$) so the bus stays clamped at $V_{\text{clamp}} = 28.0\text{ V}$, and verify the 4-bit rolling-counter + watchdog detector across normal, dropped, and frozen CAN-FD frames.

import math

# 1. Unclamped regenerative voltage surge vs Active Shunt Brake Chopper sizing:
V_nom, V_clamp = 24.0, 28.0
J_kgm2, omega0_rads, tau_max_nm, eta = 0.04, 30.0, 8.0, 0.75
C_bus_f = 1000e-6

E_regen_j = eta * 0.5 * J_kgm2 * (omega0_rads ** 2)  # 13.5 J
V_unclamped = math.sqrt(V_nom**2 + (2.0 * E_regen_j) / C_bus_f)
P_regen_peak_w = eta * tau_max_nm * omega0_rads      # 180.0 W
R_brake_max_ohm = (V_clamp ** 2) / P_regen_peak_w    # 4.3556 Ohm -> select 4.0 Ohm power resistor!
R_brake_sel_ohm = 4.0
I_brake_peak_a = V_clamp / R_brake_sel_ohm           # 7.0 A

assert math.isclose(E_regen_j, 13.5, rel_tol=1e-9)
assert math.isclose(V_unclamped, math.sqrt(27576.0), rel_tol=1e-9)  # 166.06 V!
assert math.isclose(P_regen_peak_w, 180.0, rel_tol=1e-9)
assert R_brake_sel_ohm <= R_brake_max_ohm
assert math.isclose(I_brake_peak_a, 7.0, rel_tol=1e-9)

# 2. CAN-FD 4-bit rolling counter (mod 16) & watchdog timeout check:
def check_rolling_counter(prev_c: int, curr_c: int, max_drop: int = 2) -> str:
    delta = (curr_c - prev_c) % 16
    if delta == 1:
        return "OK"
    if delta == 0:
        return "FAULT_FROZEN"
    if delta - 1 <= max_drop:
        return f"WARN_DROPPED_{delta - 1}"
    return "FAULT_SEQ_JUMP"

assert check_rolling_counter(15, 0) == "OK"              # Clean wrap 15 -> 0
assert check_rolling_counter(4, 4) == "FAULT_FROZEN"     # Duplicate/stale frame
assert check_rolling_counter(4, 6) == "WARN_DROPPED_1"   # Counter 5 was lost (1 drop)
assert check_rolling_counter(4, 10) == "FAULT_SEQ_JUMP"  # 5 drops > max_drop=2
print(f"V_unclamped={V_unclamped:.1f} V, R_brake_max={R_brake_max_ohm:.2f} Ohm, I_brake={I_brake_peak_a:.1f} A")
V_unclamped=166.1 V, R_brake_max=4.36 Ohm, I_brake=7.0 A

Edit it, then run the tests the way CI does:

The tests are behavioural: the worked $13.5\text{ J}$ and $166.06\text{ V}$; the resistor bound of $4.3556\ \Omega$ with $4.0$ inside it and $4.5$ outside; every counter outcome including the rollover and a three-frame jump; the watchdog as **frames times period**; and the HIL ratio with a refusal for an empty catalog. Four planted faults - `regen_no_eta`, `bus_linear`, `counter_plain_delta`, `watchdog_uses_period` - each fail the test named for them. The transfer suite sizes the chopper from the **shared plant**: the elbow is spun up under `plant.TAU_LIMIT`, its measured kinetic energy drives the bus surge past $28\text{ V}$, the resistor bound is tight at the peak, and the rolling counter runs over the plant's 1 kHz frame cadence, where a frame dropped every seven is a `WARN_DROPPED_1` and a stuck transmitter is a `FAULT_FROZEN`.

blocks.x: **Expected numbers (the answer):** $V_{\text{bus,unclamped}} = 169.9882\ \text{V}$ (printed as $170.0\ \text{V}$) for $48.0\ \text{V}$ plus $6.648\ \text{J}$ into $500\ \mu\text{F}$; $R_{\text{brake,max}} = 10.816\ \Omega$ at a $52.0\ \text{V}$ clamp and $250.0\ \text{W}$; a $15 \to 0$ counter step is `OK`, $4 \to 4$ is `FAULT_FROZEN`, $4 \to 6$ is `WARN_DROPPED_1`, $4 \to 10$ is `FAULT_SEQ_JUMP`.

items.x: **Energy first, then the square.** $48.0^2 = 2304$ and $2 \times 6.648 / 500\times10^{-6} = 26\,592$, so $\sqrt{28\,896} = 169.9882\ \text{V}$: the surge can only *raise* the bus, so a result below $48\ \text{V}$ means the energy term was divided instead of added.

**The resistor bound is an upper limit.** $P = V^2/R$, so $R_{\max} = 52.0^2/250.0 = 10.816\ \Omega$; a *larger* resistor cannot absorb the peak power at the clamp voltage, which is why a $12\ \Omega$ part sits outside the bound while $8\ \Omega$ sits inside.
**The counter is modulo 16, always.** `(curr - prev) % 16` maps $15 \to 0$ to $1$ (`OK`); plain subtraction gives $-15$ and turns a healthy wrap into a fault every sixteen frames at $1\ \text{kHz}$.

**Read the three verdicts off the same step.** $\Delta = 0$ is frozen, $\Delta = 1$ is `OK`, and $\Delta - 1$ is the number of dropped frames: $4 \to 6$ gives $\Delta = 2$, one drop; $4 \to 10$ gives $\Delta = 6$, five drops, past `max_drop = 2`.

**Watchdog and coverage are products and ratios.** $T_{\text{wdg}} = N_{\text{miss}} T_{\text{cmd}} = 3 \times 1.0\ \text{ms} = 3.0\ \text{ms}$; $C_{\text{HIL}} = F_{\text{passed}}/F_{\text{total}}$ and an empty catalogue must raise rather than divide by zero.

**What the suite refuses.** `unclamped_bus_v` refuses a zero bus capacitance, `brake_resistor_max_ohm` refuses a peak power of zero (with no power there is no bound a resistor could meet), and `hil_coverage` refuses an empty fault catalogue - the case item 5 warns about, checked by the suite - each with `ValueError`.

blocks.x: Inject the `counter_plain_delta` fault and diagnose it from the frame log alone, keeping the $1\text{ kHz}$ command cadence:

items.x: **Inject:** compute the counter step as plain signed subtraction, `delta = curr_c - prev_c`, instead of modulo-16 arithmetic `(curr_c - prev_c) % 16` (the wrap bug in `## 8. Common mistakes`).

**Symptom:** the clean wrap $15 \to 0$ yields $-15$, which is `<= max_drop` in a naive `delta - 1 <= max_drop` test, so a perfectly healthy frame stream is reported as `WARN_DROPPED_-16`; with the guard written the other way it is reported as `FAULT_SEQ_JUMP` instead. Either way the fault appears once every $16\text{ ms}$ at $1\text{ kHz}$, i.e. $62.5$ times per second, so a drive that latches on any non-`OK` verdict trips continuously while the transmitter is behaving correctly.

**Diagnose:** the wrap is the only place the two arithmetics disagree. A frozen frame $4 \to 4$ gives $0$ both ways and a one-frame drop $4 \to 6$ gives $2$ both ways, so a verdict that is correct for every non-wrapping pair and wrong only at $15 \to 0$ localises the bug to the missing modulus - not to the CRC, the watchdog window, or a genuinely stuck node.

**Fix:** restore the modular step `(curr_c - prev_c) % 16` (or `& 0x0F`) and prove it on the four cases the worked example already asserts: $15 \to 0$ is `OK`, $4 \to 4$ is `FAULT_FROZEN`, $4 \to 6$ is `WARN_DROPPED_1`, and $4 \to 10$ is `FAULT_SEQ_JUMP`. The planted fault must fail `test_behavior`, and the plant-cadence transfer check must pass.

items.x: **Hazard:** Regenerative over-voltage capacitor explosion ($>160\text{ V}$ spike on a $24\text{ V}$ bus during fast deceleration), exposed hot brake-chopper power resistors ($>150^\circ\text{C}$ under repetitive braking), and runaway actuator motion on stale CAN-FD commands.

**Mitigation:** Always verify the shunt brake chopper threshold ($V_{\text{on}} = 27.5\text{ V}$) with an adjustable bench supply before commanding high-speed deceleration, mount the wirewound brake resistor in an insulated heatsink cage with software $I^2t$ duty-cycle derating, and enforce a $3\text{ ms}$ hardware watchdog timeout that disables PWM or switches to passive damping on missed CAN frames.

`[Concept: regenerative_bus_energy_and_chopper_sizing]` If the hysteretic brake chopper turns ON at $V_{\text{on}} = 28.0\text{ V}$ and turns OFF at $V_{\text{off}} = 26.0\text{ V}$, compute the hysteresis band width $\Delta V_{\text{hyst}} = V_{\text{on}} - V_{\text{off}}$ in Volts ($\text{V}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}\text{ V}$).

`[Concept: can_fd_crc16_and_rolling_counter_watchdog]` A CAN-FD actuator expects $500\text{ Hz}$ command packets ($T_{\text{cmd}} = 2.0\text{ ms}$) and latches a communication timeout fault after $N_{\text{miss}} = 3$ consecutive missed packets. Compute the watchdog timeout window $T_{\text{wdg}} = N_{\text{miss}} \cdot T_{\text{cmd}}$ in milliseconds ($\text{ms}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}\text{ ms}$).

`[Concept: can_fd_crc16_and_rolling_counter_watchdog]` Why must safety-critical CAN-FD actuator frames include **both** a 16-bit CRC and a 4-bit rolling counter (`0..15`), rather than relying on the CRC alone?

**A.** A valid CRC only proves the bytes were not corrupted in transit; the rolling counter detects **frozen/stale buffer replay** (where a crashed host repeatedly transmits the exact same valid packet with a valid CRC) and counts dropped frames.
**B.** The 4-bit rolling counter doubles the CAN bus voltage.
**C.** CRC-16 only works on odd-numbered days.
**D.** Rolling counters replace termination resistors.

`[Concept: sil_hil_fault_injection_verification]` Across $F_{\text{total}} = 8$ mandatory Tier 2 HIL fault-injection tests, your drive passes $F_{\text{passed}} = 8$ within the reaction budget. If the allowed over-current reaction budget is $t_{\text{budget}} = 50.0\ \mu\text{s}$ and the measured hardware comparator trip time is $t_{\text{react}} = 1.5\ \mu\text{s}$, compute the safety timing margin $t_{\text{margin}} = t_{\text{budget}} - t_{\text{react}}$ in microseconds ($\mu\text{s}$, tolerance $\pm 10^{-9}\ \mu\text{s}$).
`[Concept: sil_hil_fault_injection_verification]` What is the safest fallback action for a backdrivable QDD robot joint (`MIT Mode`) when the CAN-FD command watchdog times out during a fast swing?

**A.** Immediately zero the feedforward torque and position stiffness ($K_p = 0, \tau_{\text{ff}} = 0$) and apply pure passive/viscous damping ($\tau = -K_{d,\text{safe}} \dot{q}$) before asserting Safe Torque Off once velocity decays near zero.
**B.** Hold the last commanded torque $\tau_{\text{ff}}$ forever at $100\%$ duty cycle.

rows: Brake chopper MOSFET chatters at $50text{ kHz}$ and overheats around the trip threshold
Used a zero-hysteresis threshold ($V_{text{on}} = V_{text{off}} = 27.5text{ V}$), so the bus voltage bounces up and down across the threshold on every microsecond.
Implement a Schmitt-trigger hysteresis band ($V_{text{on}} = 27.5text{ V}, V_{text{off}} = 25.5text{ V}$) so the chopper stays cleanly ON until the bus discharges by $2text{ V}$.
Shunt brake resistor smokes during continuous oscillatory trajectory tracking
Sized the resistor's Ohm value for peak power ($4 Omega$) but used a tiny $5text{ W}$ resistor without software $I^2t$ duty-cycle protection.

Use a chassis-mounted $50text{–}100text{ W}$ aluminum-housed wirewound resistor and track cumulative chopper ON-time in software to derate speed if average braking power exceeds the continuous rating.
CAN-FD watchdog triggers false timeouts when the rolling counter wraps from `15` to `0`
Computed signed subtraction `curr_c - prev_c` (`0 - 15 = -15`) instead of unsigned modulo-16 arithmetic `(curr_c - prev_c) & 0x0F`.
Always compute `(curr_c - prev_c) & 0x0F == 1` so `15 -> 0` evaluates to `(-15) & 0x0F = 1`.
